extracted.intended_audience: students of Euclidean geometry / mathematics students studying Book V–VI of Euclid
extracted.subtask_description: Focused study of Euclid's Book V (theory of proportion: ratios, proportionals, equimultiples, incommensurables, and propositions I–XXV) and the opening of Book VI (application to similar figures). Intended as study/reference material for students learning the theory of proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraction (Definition I)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an integer be divided into any number of equal parts, one, or the sum of any number of these parts, is called a fraction. A fraction is denoted by two numbers parted by a horizontal line; the lower (denominator) denotes the number of equal parts into which the integer is divided; the upper (numerator) denotes the number of these equal parts taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given using division of a line AB into 4 parts: AC = 1/4, AD = 2/4, AE = 3/4. If numerator < denominator fraction < 1; if equal, = 1; if greater, > 1. A fraction is an abstract quantity independent of the physical nature of the unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariant transformations of a fraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Two transformations can be made on any fraction without changing its value: multiply both numerator and denominator by any whole number, or divide both by any whole number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: multiplying numerator and denominator by 2 transforms 1/4 to 2/8 without altering value. Conversely dividing terms by a common whole number preserves value. This is presented as an important and fundamental theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple / Submultiple / Measure (Definition III)
rubrics_metrics.description: If we take any number and multiply it by any whole number, the product is called a multiple of the original number. Conversely, the original number is a submultiple (or measure or part) of its multiples — it is contained in them without remainder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: multiples of 3 are 6,9,12,...; numbers like 10,13 are not multiples of 3 because multiplication by a whole number does not produce them. Terminology: 'measure' = submultiple.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratio (Definition IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ratio is the mutual relation of two magnitudes of the same kind with respect to quantity. Two magnitudes are said to have a ratio to one another when the less can be multiplied so as to exceed the greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For commensurable magnitudes, a ratio 3:4 corresponds to the fraction 3/4 and to numerical measures with the same unit. Every ratio of commensurable magnitudes can be converted into a fraction, and every fraction into a ratio. Ratios of incommensurable magnitudes are treated via limiting approximations (convergents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incommensurable ratios and convergents
rubrics_metrics.description: When two quantities are incommensurable (e.g., side and diagonal of a square), their ratio is not equal to any ratio of commensurable numbers, but a sequence of pairs of fractions (convergents) can be found whose differences diminish indefinitely and between which the true ratio lies; thus the ratio may be regarded as the limit of ratios of commensurable quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated with side a and diagonal b of a square; explanation that for any large n one can find fractions bracketing the true ratio, and the difference can be made arbitrarily small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antecedent and consequent; ratio as fraction (Definition V)
rubrics_metrics.description: The two terms of a ratio are called the antecedent and the consequent; these correspond to numerator and denominator of a fraction. A ratio is the fraction obtained by making the antecedent the numerator and the consequent the denominator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology mapping between ratio notation (a:b) and fractional notation a/b. Clarifies language used subsequently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal of a ratio (Definition VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reciprocal of a ratio is obtained by interchanging antecedent and consequent. Example: 4:3 is the reciprocal of 3:4. The product of a ratio and its reciprocal is unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple properties of inversion (reciprocals) and their multiplicative relation to 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equimultiples (Definition VII)
rubrics_metrics.description: If we multiply any two numbers (or magnitudes) by the same number we obtain equimultiples of those numbers. Equimultiples are corresponding multiples formed by multiplying each term by the same multiplier(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 5 and 7 multiplied by 4 give equimultiples 20 and 28. The concept is central to Euclid's treatment of equality of ratios via comparison of equimultiples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of ratios by equimultiples (Euclid's Definition V / fundamental test)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first of four magnitudes has to the second the same ratio which the third has to the fourth when, for any equimultiples whatsoever of the first and third and any equimultiples whatsoever of the second and fourth, the comparison of the multiples of the first and second (greater/equal/less) matches the comparison of the multiples of the third and fourth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Euclid's fundamental (and non-numeric) definition of equality of ratios: equality is tested by the behaviour of all equimultiples. It underlies many propositions and is used both for commensurable and incommensurable cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion and proportion notation
rubrics_metrics.description: When two ratios are asserted equal, this assertion is called a proportion, written a:b :: c:d or a:b = c:d. The four terms are two antecedents (1st and 3rd) and two consequents (2nd and 4th); extremes = first and last terms; means = the two middle terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proportions can be written as equality of fractions, and conversely an equality between fractions can be stated as a proportion. This equivalence is used to derive properties of proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion between proportion and equality of fractions
rubrics_metrics.description: A proportion a:b :: c:d can be written as equality of fractions a/b = c/d; conversely an equality of fractions can be put into proportional form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly to translate ratio/proportion statements into algebraic fraction equalities for proofs and manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of deriving new proportions (multiplying terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a:b :: c:d, and we multiply the first and third each by m and the second and fourth each by n, then ma:nb :: mc:nd; and comparisons (greater/equal/less) carry over similarly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof given by multiplying equal fractions and reasoning about whether results exceed unity. This justifies forming new proportions by scaling terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclid's theorem: equimultiples comparisons imply equal ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: If, whenever equimultiples are taken of the first and third and of the second and fourth magnitudes, then according as the multiple of the first is greater than/equal to/less than that of the second, the multiple of the third is respectively greater/equal/less than that of the fourth, then the ratio of the first to the second equals the ratio of the third to the fourth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof treats commensurable case by finding exact multiples, and incommensurable case via convergent approximations; shows Euclid's definition is sufficient to conclude equality of ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: proportion consists of three terms at least (annotation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion consists of three terms at least is an inference rather than a strict definition — arises when the means in a proportion are equal (e.g., continued proportion 4:6 :: 6:9 actually has four terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains historical peculiarity in Euclid's wording and clarifies that actual proportions may have four terms even when described as 'three terms'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounded, duplicate and triplicate ratios (Defs x, xi, xii)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ratio compounded of several ratios is the ratio of the product of all antecedents to the product of all consequents. The duplicate ratio (of 1st to 3rd) is the square of the ratio (i.e., ratio of squares); the triplicate ratio is the cube; in general compound ratio is the product of component ratios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ratios 5:7 and 3:4 compound to 15:28. If a:b :: b:c then a:c is the square of a:b (duplicate). These definitions are used to define repeated/compounded ratios explicitly via products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homologous terms in proportionals
rubrics_metrics.description: In proportionals, antecedent terms are called homologous to one another, and likewise the consequents are homologous to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives compact language for stating derived proportions and transformations of proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition I (Book V)
rubrics_metrics.description: If any number of magnitudes of the same kind (a, b, c, ...) be equimultiples of as many others (a', b', c', ...), then the sum of the first magnitudes (a + b + c + ...) shall be the same multiple of the sum of the second which any magnitude of the first system is of the corresponding magnitude of the second system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: denote common multiple m so that a = m a', b = m b', ... then add to show sum relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition II (Book V)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two magnitudes a, b are the same multiples of another c which two corresponding magnitudes a', b' are of another c', then the sum a + b is the same multiple of c that a' + b' is of c'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via representing a = m c and b = n c and showing sum corresponds similarly for a' and b'. Statement generalizes to any number of multiples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition III (Book V)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two magnitudes a, b be equimultiples of two others a', b'; then any equimultiples of the first magnitudes na, nb will also be equimultiples of the second magnitudes na', nb'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trivial scaling argument: if a = m a', b = m b' then multiply each by n to preserve equimultiple relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition IV (Book V)
rubrics_metrics.description: If four magnitudes be proportional (a:b :: c:d), and if any equimultiples of the first and third be taken, and any other equimultiples of the second and fourth, then ma:nb :: mc:nd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses fraction equality and multiplication of numerators/denominators by the multipliers to obtain new proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition V (Book V)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two magnitudes a, b be the same multiples of another c which two corresponding magnitudes a', b' are of another c', then the difference a - b is the same multiple of c that a' - b' is of c'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent a = m c, b = n c and analogous for a', b' to obtain difference relation (a - b) = (m - n) c.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition VI (Book V)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a magnitude a be the same multiple of another b, which a' (a part of the first) is of b' (a part of the second), then the remainder a - a' is the same multiple of the remainder b - b' that the whole is of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic representation a = m b, a' = m b' gives (a - a') = m (b - b').

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition A (Simson) (Book V)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two ratios be equal (a:b :: c:d), then according as the antecedent of the first is greater than/equal to/less than its consequent, the antecedent of the second is respectively greater/equal/less than its consequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses fraction interpretation: if a/b > 1 then c/d > 1, etc. Gives monotonicity of equality-of-ratios with respect to inequality between antecedent and consequent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition B (Simson) (invertendo)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two ratios are equal their reciprocals are equal: a:b :: c:d implies b:a :: d:c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by inverting fractions 1/(a/b) etc. Standard operation 'invertendo'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition C (Simson)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the first of four magnitudes be the same multiple of the second which the third is of the fourth, the first is to the second as the third is to the fourth (i.e., common multiplier implies proportionality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate from equal multipliers: if a = m b and c = m d then a:b :: c:d.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition D (Simson)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a:b :: c:d and a is a multiple (or submultiple) of b, then c is the same multiple (or submultiple) of d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two parts: if a = m b then c = m d; if a is a submultiple then similar; uses fraction equality and substitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition VII (Book V)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) Equal magnitudes have equal ratios to the same magnitude. 2) The same magnitude has equal ratios to equal magnitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct: if a = b then a:c :: b:c and c:a :: c:b. Observation: second follows from first by inversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition VIII (Book V)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) Of two unequal magnitudes, the greater has a greater ratio to any third magnitude than the less has. 2) Any third magnitude has a greater ratio to the less of two unequal magnitudes than it has to the greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by division/quotients: dividing a and b by the same c yields larger quotient for larger numerator; conversely dividing c by smaller denominator gives larger quotient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition IX (Book V)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) Magnitudes which have equal ratios to the same magnitude are equal to one another. 2) Magnitudes to which the same magnitude has equal ratios are equal to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a:c :: b:c then a = b by multiplying both sides by c. Second follows by inversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition X (Book V)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) Of two unequal magnitudes, that which has the greater ratio to any third is the greater of the two. 2) That to which any third has the greater ratio is the less of the two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relates comparisons of ratios back to comparisons of magnitudes using multiplication by the third magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XI (Book V)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ratios that are equal to the same ratio are equal to one another: if a:b :: e:f and c:d :: e:f then a:b :: c:d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transitivity of ratio equality via common comparison to e:f and Axiom I (equality of equals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XII (Book V)
rubrics_metrics.description: If any number of ratios be equal to one another, any one of these equal ratios is equal to the ratio of the sum of all the antecedents to the sum of all the consequents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a/b = c/d = e/f = r then a + c + e = r (b + d + f), so (a + c + e):(b + d + f) = r. Corollary: linear combinations with multipliers preserve proportionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XIII (Book V)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two ratios are equal, and if one of them be greater than any third ratio, then the other is also greater than that third ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monotonicity: from a:b :: c:d and c:d > e:f infer a:b > e:f by substitution/comparison of fractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XIV (Book V)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two ratios be equal, then, according as the antecedent of the first is greater/equal/less than the antecedent of the second, the consequence of the first is respectively greater/equal/less than the consequent of the second.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From a:b :: c:d, comparing a and c leads to corresponding comparison of b and d (preserves inequality correspondences). Uses prior propositions and fraction algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XV (Book V)
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnitudes have the same ratio which all equimultiples of them have: a:b :: ma:mb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because multiplying numerator and denominator by same number leaves fraction value unchanged; direct consequence of the invariant transformation of fractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XVI (Book V) (alternando)
rubrics_metrics.description: If four magnitudes of the same kind be proportionals they are also proportionals by alternation: a:b :: c:d implies a:c :: b:d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Established by algebraic manipulation of fractions; gives the alternando transformation of proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XVII (Book V) (dividendo)
rubrics_metrics.description: If four magnitudes be proportionals, the difference between the first and second : the second :: the difference between the third and fourth : the fourth (i.e., a - b : b :: c - d : d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by subtracting 1 from fractions (a/b - 1 etc.) and manipulating to get the new proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XVIII (Book V) (componendo)
rubrics_metrics.description: If four magnitudes be proportionals, the sum of the first and second : the second :: the sum of the third and fourth : the fourth (i.e., a + b : b :: c + d : d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add 1 to both fractions a/b, c/d to get (a + b)/b etc.; standard componendo rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XIX (Book V)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a whole magnitude be to another whole as a magnitude taken from the first is to a magnitude taken from the second, then the remainder of the first : remainder of the second :: first whole : second whole (i.e., a - c : b - d :: a : b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses alternando and invertendo on proportions and algebraic rearrangement to derive the relation between remainders and wholes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition E (Simson) (convertendo)
rubrics_metrics.description: If four magnitudes be proportional, the first : its excess above the second :: the third : its excess above the fourth (a : a - b :: c : c - d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses prior proposition [xvii] and division to obtain convertendo relation; helps transform comparisons about differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions XX–XXIII (Book V): chain/transverse equalities and ex aequali
rubrics_metrics.description: XX–XXIII establish that if two sets of three magnitudes taken two by two in direct or transverse order have equal ratios, then corresponding order relations (greater/equal/less) are preserved across sets, and that compounded ratios of equal ratios are equal (ex aequali and ex aequo / ex aequo perturbato).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They formalize transitivity and composition of equal ratios over chains of magnitudes; proofs use multiplying equal fractions and transitivity arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XXIV (Book V)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two magnitudes a, b have to a third c ratios equal to those which two other magnitudes a', b' have to c', then the sum a + b has to c the same ratio which a' + b' has to c'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by adding equal fractions a/c = a'/c' and b/c = b'/c' to obtain (a + b)/c = (a' + b')/c'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XXV (Book V)
rubrics_metrics.description: If four magnitudes of the same kind be proportionals, the sum of the greatest and least is greater than the sum of the other two (i.e., if a:b :: c:d and a is greatest and d least, then a + d > b + c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses alternando, convertendo and earlier inequality propositions to compare differences and conclude the inequality of sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions for Examination on Book V (study checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of study/examination questions enumerating the subject-matter and key points the student should know about Book V: subject matter; definition of multiple/submultiple/equimultiples; ratio of commensurable and incommensurable magnitudes; terms of a ratio; ratio of greater/lesser inequality; product/compound of ratios; duplicate/triplicate ratio; what is proportion; Euclid's definition of proportion; how many ratios in a proportion; Latin technical terms; harmonic division; reciprocal ratios; etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as an explicit checklist of topics the student should be able to answer and recall; the page lists 23+ specific questions and short answers/hints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercises on Book V (exercise problems and properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: A collection of exercises and short propositions to be proved or shown, including formal definitions of ratio inequality effects, componendo et dividendo, properties of proportional sets, continued proportional properties, harmonic division problems, and several algebraic/geometry identities related to proportional divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: show how ratios change when terms are increased/decreased by same quantity; if four magnitudes are proportional the sum and difference relations (componendo/dividendo); proving squares and cubes of proportionals are proportional; harmonic division geometric exercises (OC, OB, OD continual proportionals); and various algebraic equalities derived from harmonic cuts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book VI: Definitions — Similar rectilineal figures (Book VI Def i)
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar rectilineal figures are those whose several angles are equal, each to each, and whose sides about the equal angles are proportional. Similar figures agree in shape; if they also agree in size they are congruent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks on species (shape), magnitude (size), and position. Introduces the terminology and conceptual link between proportion theory and similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book VI: Def ii–vi (mean proportional, extreme and mean ratio notions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions include: (ii) extreme and mean ratio for a line cut in extreme and mean ratio (golden section style), (iii) mean proportional (middle term in continued proportion), (iv) two mean proportionals for four quantities in continued proportion, (v) altitude = perpendicular from highest point to base of figure, (vi) reciprocal proportionality of sides about corresponding angles (sides reciprocally proportional meaning side of first to side of second = reciprocal of remaining sides ratio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions set up the vocabulary needed for applying proportion theory to similar figures, including mean proportionals (geometric progression) and technical language used in later propositions of Book VI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition I (Book VI application theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Triangles (ABC, ACD) and parallelograms (EC, CF) which have the same altitude are to one another as their bases (BC : CD :: area(ABC) : area(ACD)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via dividing bases into equal parts and comparing equimultiple triangles; or via area formula A = P * base. Extends to parallelograms by same altitude argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition II (Book VI: parallel line proportionality)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a line DE be parallel to side BC of triangle ABC, it divides the remaining sides, measured from the opposite angle A, proportionally: AD:DB :: AE:EC; conversely, if two sides measured from an angle are cut proportionally, the line joining the points is parallel to the third side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses equality of triangles between same parallels and base and previously established proportionality of triangles to their bases; this is the fundamental similarity / intercept theorem.
